summary: This unit helps you work out whether, when and how to start your own small business in your trade. You will learn what makes an entrepreneur, how to judge yourself and a business idea with a SWOT analysis and market research, and how to set SMART goals. You will also learn to cost and price your work, find start-up money, set up legally in Jamaica, market the business, keep records and manage risk, and turn it all into a written plan for your own path from trainee to business owner.

blocks.p: This unit is shared by several Level 2 programmes at the Centre, including welding, electrical installation, cosmetology, beauty therapy and hospitality (villa and property services). It is about **entrepreneurship**: starting and running your own business. It does not ask you to open a business now. It asks you to plan a sensible path towards one, so that if you do start, you start well.

Many skilled people in Jamaica work for themselves: the welder who makes grills and gates, the electrician who wires houses, the nail technician, the barber, the housekeeper who looks after holiday villas. Some do it full time; many start with jobs at weekends. Good trade skills are not enough on their own. A business also needs customers, prices that cover the costs, records, and a plan.

**Who it is for:** any trainee who may one day work for themselves, or who wants to understand how the business they work for makes its money. The examples come from several trades, so use the ones closest to yours.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Explain what an entrepreneur is
Say how working for yourself differs from being employed, and which personal qualities help a business succeed.
Know yourself
Use a SWOT analysis to look honestly at your strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, and decide what you need before you start.
Set goals
Write SMART goals for your skills, your savings and your business.
Find and test an idea
Spot a need that customers will pay to have met, then check it with simple market research and a look at the competition.
Plan the money
Work out start-up costs, fixed and variable costs, prices, profit and break-even, and plan your cash flow and funding.
Set up properly
Choose a type of business, register it, have a TRN, and know which taxes, licences and insurance apply.
Win and keep customers
Use the four Ps, low-cost promotion, written quotations and good service, and build a network of contacts.
Run the business with care
Keep records, keep business and personal money apart, manage risk and act honestly.
Write your plan
Put it all into a simple business plan and a personal strategy, and review them as you go.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on entrepreneurs, SWOT, goals, market research, costs, prices, profit, funding, setting up legally, marketing, records and risk.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as capital, interest, invoice, deposit and stock, and simple money sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two group practicals.** In the first, your group writes a short customer survey, asks people at the Centre, counts the answers on a tally sheet, makes a SWOT poster and decides whether to go ahead with, change or drop the idea. In the second, your group makes a start-up budget, lists fixed and variable costs, sets prices for three services and writes a quotation for a sample job.

blocks.note: Bring a calculator to every session. Many questions ask you to work out a profit, a price or a total. Show your working, and check every sum a second way.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Money in this kit is in Jamaican dollars (J$). Exam papers may write just $; it means the same.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: An **entrepreneur** is a person who starts and runs a business and takes the risk. They spend their own time and money before they know for sure that it will pay. If the business does well, they keep the profit; if it fails, they carry the loss.

Employed
Self-employed

An employer: a boss, a company or a government body
Yourself; in a way, your customers are your boss
How you are paid
A fixed wage or salary on a set day
Whatever the business earns after its costs: more in some months, less in others
Risk
Low: you are paid even if the business has a slow month
High: you can lose your savings if the business fails
Hours
Set by the employer
As long as the work needs, often evenings and weekends at first
Decisions

Made by you
Finding work

You register and pay your own contributions, and have no paid leave unless you save for it

What it looks like

Willing to take sensible risks

Determined and hard-working

Keeps learning

blocks.h: For and against working for yourself

head: Good points
Hard points
rows: You make the decisions
You keep the profit
You can build something that grows and employs others
Flexible hours, once the business is settled
Income is not steady
You can lose your savings
Long hours, especially at the start
No paid sick days or holidays unless you plan for them
You must do the paperwork, the selling and the trade work

blocks.p: Fair, honest dealing is good business. In a Jamaican town, word of a cheat travels fast, and word of good, honest work brings steady customers.

ul: Give a written quotation and stick to it. If something must change, explain it and agree it with the customer **before** you do it.
Use the materials and products the customer paid for, never cheaper ones in their place.
Charge everyone a fair price for the same work. Do not secretly charge visitors or tourists more.
Tell the customer about any fault in the work; do not hide it.
Pay suppliers and workers on time, and keep your promises on dates.
Compete on quality, price and service. Never spread untrue stories about a competitor.

blocks.note: Many Jamaican tradespeople begin with "side jobs" while they are still employed. It is a good way to test an idea, if your employer's rules allow it. Never take your employer's customers, tools or materials, and never do private jobs in work time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Knowing yourself: SWOT, goals and your personal strategy

blocks.p: A **SWOT analysis** is a simple way to look honestly at yourself, or at a business idea, before you start. You draw four boxes and fill each one. Strengths and weaknesses are **inside** you or your business. Opportunities and threats are **outside**: you cannot control them, but you can plan for them.

head: Letter
Means
Inside or outside?
Examples
rows: S
Strengths: what you are good at or already have
Inside
Your NVQ-J certificate; neat, strong work; your own tools; some savings; a good name with customers
W
Weaknesses: what you lack or do badly
Inside
Little experience in pricing; no transport; weak record keeping; shy with new customers
O
Opportunities: chances outside you that could help
Outside
A new housing scheme being built nearby; more villas rented to visitors; more homes adding solar panels; a hotel opening that needs services
T
Threats: dangers outside you that could hurt
Outside
Strong competitors nearby; rising prices of steel or products; the slow season; hurricanes and power cuts; customers who do not pay

flow: Fill the four boxes honestly, and ask a friend or your instructor what they would add
Build on your strengths: make them part of what you offer and how you sell
Plan how to fix each important weakness: training, more work experience, a partner, or help from an adviser
Choose which opportunities you will go after
For each threat, write down what you will do if it happens
Decide: ready to start, start small, or not yet; and set goals for what must happen first

blocks.note: A common mistake is putting outside things in the inside boxes. "A new competitor opened next door" is a threat, not a weakness. "I cannot price a job" is a weakness, not a threat.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A goal tells you where you are going. A **SMART** goal is one you can plan for and check.

head: Letter
Meaning
Ask yourself
rows: S
Specific: says exactly what you will do
What exactly?
M
Measurable: has a number or a check, so you know when it is done
How much? How many? How will I know?
A
Achievable: possible with your skills, money and time
Can I really do it?
R
Relevant: matters for your plan
Does it move me towards my business?
T
Time-bound: has a deadline
By when?

head: Not SMART
SMART
rows: "I want to save some money."
"I will put J$10 000 from each month's pay into a separate account, so that I have J$120 000 for tools in 12 months."
"I want more customers."
"By the end of this month I will get 5 new paying customers by giving flyers to 100 homes and posting photos of my work twice a week."
"I will get better at pricing."
"By the end of March I will price 10 jobs on my supervisor's costing sheet and have each one checked by her."

blocks.p: Most successful tradespeople did not open a business on the day they qualified. They built skills, savings and contacts first, so that when they started, they knew the trade, the customers and the costs. Mistakes are cheaper to learn while someone else is paying the bills.

flow: Finish your qualification (NVQ-J or the Centre's certificate)
Work in your trade for a while and watch how the business deals with customers, pricing and suppliers
Save a fixed amount from every pay, in a separate account
Build your skills with short courses and learn basic bookkeeping
Test your idea with small jobs, keep records of them and build a list of customers
Research the market, write a business plan and work out your costs and funding
Register the business and start small, keeping your costs low
Review your plan every few months and change it when you need to

blocks.p: Once the business is running, pay yourself a **set wage** from it, for example every week or every month. This lets you plan your household spending and leaves the rest of the money in the business for materials, bills and savings. Taking cash out whenever you need it hides how the business is really doing, and can leave nothing to buy materials for the next job.

sections.title: Finding and testing a business idea

blocks.p: A **business opportunity** is a need or a problem that customers will pay to have met. An idea is only an opportunity if enough people want it, at a price that covers your costs and leaves a profit.

ul: **Complaints:** listen to what people grumble about. "Nobody round here fixes gates quickly." "I can never get a nail appointment on Sunday."
**Gaps:** services that are hard to get nearby, or have long waiting times.
**Changes:** new housing schemes, new hotels and villas, new roads, more homes going solar, new rules that need a service.
**Your own skills and contacts:** what you do best, and who already knows your work.
**Doing an old thing better:** faster, mobile, cleaner, more reliable, or with better follow-up.

blocks.note: Match the idea to your skills. A welder who is good at finishing might focus on decorative gates and rails; one who likes site work might offer a mobile repair service.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Market research** means finding out about customers, competitors and demand before you spend money. It answers: Who will buy? How many? How often? At what price? Who else sells it, and how good are they?

head: Type
What it is
Examples
rows: Primary (field) research
Information you collect yourself
A short survey of possible customers
Talking to customers and suppliers
Counting how many people pass a spot
Watching a competitor's busy times
Secondary (desk) research
Information other people have already collected
Competitors' price lists and online reviews
Reports from business-support bodies and government
Trade magazines and websites

ul: Keep it to about 6 to 8 short questions, each asking one thing.
Use mostly closed questions (tick a box) so the answers are easy to count, plus one or two open questions, such as "What would make you choose a new service?"
Ask what matters: would they use it, how often, what they would pay, and what matters most to them (price, speed, quality, being on time).
Do not lead people towards an answer. "You would pay more for quality, wouldn't you?" is a leading question.
Ask the people you hope will buy (your target market), not only family and friends, who may say yes to please you.
Be polite: say who you are and why you are asking, and accept a "no".
Do not write down phone numbers or addresses unless the person agrees and you really need them.
Count the answers on a **tally sheet** (marks in groups of five) and turn them into simple numbers or percentages.

blocks.p: Example result: of 30 homeowners asked, 21 (70%) said they would use a mobile grill-repair service at least once a year, 15 said they would pay J$3 000 to J$5 000 for a call-out, and 24 said "turning up on time" mattered most. That tells the welder what to offer, what to charge, and what to promise.

Your **target market** is the group of customers most likely to buy from you, for example homeowners in new housing schemes nearby, brides and their bridal parties, villa owners who live overseas, or small shops that need electrical repairs. Knowing them tells you where to advertise, what to charge and what to offer.

A **competitor** is another business that sells the same or similar goods or services to the same customers. Study them before you start: not to copy them or run them down, but to learn the market and find how you can do better.

head: Look at
Why
rows: Their prices
So that your prices are realistic
The quality of their work
To see what standard customers expect
Their service
Do they turn up on time, answer the phone and give written quotes?
Their location and opening hours
To spot gaps you could fill
What their customers complain about
Your chance to be better

blocks.p: A **unique selling point (USP)** is what makes your business different from the rest and gives customers a reason to choose you. Examples: "Same-day call-out for broken grills and gates"; "Home nail service for bridal parties, any day of the week"; "Villa cleaning with a photo report sent to the overseas owner after every visit". A low price alone is a weak USP, because someone can always charge less.

Before you spend a lot, test the idea on a small scale: a few weekend jobs, a stall at a community event, or offering the service to a few customers. Keep records of what each job cost and earned and what customers said. Then decide, and write down why: **go ahead**, **change the idea**, or **drop it**.

head: Cost
What it is
Examples from several trades
rows: Start-up costs
One-off costs to open the business
Welding machine, grinder and hand tools
Salon chair, nail lamp, steriliser
Ladders, test meters and tools
First stock, sign, registration, deposit on a room
Fixed costs
Running costs that stay the same each month, whatever the amount of work
Rent
Insurance
Loan repayments
Phone and internet plan
A helper on a fixed monthly wage
Variable costs
Running costs that go up and down with the amount of work
Steel, rods, discs and paint for each gate
Cable and fittings for each job
Nail products, cotton and towels for each client
Cleaning products for each villa
Overheads
Running costs of the whole business, not tied to one job
Rent, electricity, phone
Transport
Wear on tools
Accountant's fees

blocks.note: Electricity is partly fixed and partly variable: you pay some of it however busy you are, and more when machines run longer. At this level, treat it as an overhead and include a share of it in every price.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Sales turnover** (sales income) is all the money received from sales, before any costs are taken off.
**Profit** is the money left after all the costs are paid: profit = sales income − total costs.
If the costs are more than the income, the result is a **loss**.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** In March, Keisha's home salon takes in J$186 000 from 62 clients. Her fixed costs are rent J$35 000, phone J$4 000 and insurance J$3 000: J$42 000. Her products cost about J$1 100 per client: 62 × J$1 100 = J$68 200. Total costs = J$42 000 + J$68 200 = J$110 200. Profit = J$186 000 − J$110 200 = **J$75 800**.

flow: List the direct costs of the job: materials and consumables
Add the labour: your time, and any helper's, at a fair hourly rate
Add a share of the overheads: rent, electricity, transport, wear on tools
This is the total cost. Add a profit, often as a percentage of the cost
Check what competitors charge and what customers will pay; adjust if needed, but never below your total cost
Give the customer a written quotation

head: Working out a quote: a 1.2 m × 2.0 m security grille
Amount
rows: Steel, rods, grinding discs, primer and paint
Labour: 8 hours at J$1 500 an hour
Share of overheads (transport, electricity, tool wear)
Total cost
Profit at 20% of the cost: J$40 000 × 0.20
Price to quote

blocks.p: To add a percentage in one step, multiply by (100 + the percentage) ÷ 100. For 20%: J$40 000 × 1.20 = J$48 000.

blocks.note: Charging less than a job costs you is not a bargain for the business: every such job loses money. If your price is far above everyone else's, look again at your costs and how you work, rather than just cutting out the profit.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: If the business is registered for General Consumption Tax (GCT), GCT is added to the price at the current rate and paid over to Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ). Ask TAJ or an accountant whether your business must register.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The **break-even point** is where income just covers all the costs: no profit and no loss. Below it you lose money; above it you make a profit. To find how many jobs or clients you need each month:

ol: Work out how much each job contributes: its price minus its variable cost.
Divide the monthly fixed costs by that amount.
Round up to a whole number of jobs.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A barber's fixed costs are J$60 000 a month. A haircut costs J$1 500, and its variable cost (products, blades, towel washing) is J$300. Each cut contributes J$1 500 − J$300 = J$1 200. Break-even = J$60 000 ÷ J$1 200 = **50 haircuts a month**. The 51st haircut is the first one that makes a profit.

blocks.note: If the answer is not a whole number, round up: you cannot sell part of a haircut. 46.2 jobs means 47 jobs to break even.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Cash flow** is the money coming into and going out of the business, and when. A business can make a profit on paper and still run out of cash, for example when it buys steel for a big job in May but the customer pays only at the end of June. Meanwhile the rent and the phone bill still have to be paid.

head: Month (cash at the start of April: J$50 000)
Cash in
Cash out
Cash at the end of the month
rows: April
May: steel bought for a hotel railing job
−J$20 000 (short)
June: the hotel pays

blocks.p: May shows a shortfall, even though the hotel job will make a profit. To manage cash flow: take a **deposit** before a big job starts, agree payments at stages of the work, ask suppliers for credit, keep some cash in reserve, chase customers who owe you, and plan big purchases.

Money put into a business to start it is called **capital**. The money the owner puts in from their own savings is the owner's capital. Work out how much you need: all the start-up costs, plus enough to pay the running costs for the first few months while customers build up.

head: Source
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Personal savings
Nothing to pay back; no interest; you keep full control
Takes time to build up; you can lose them if the business fails
A **loan** from a bank, credit union or small-business lender
A larger amount, quickly; repayments can be planned
Must be paid back with interest, even in a slow month; the lender usually wants a business plan, records and security
Family or friends
May be cheaper and more flexible
Disagreements over money can spoil relationships; agree the terms in writing
A partner who puts money in
Brings money and often skills and contacts too
Profits and decisions are shared; you need a written agreement
Grants and support programmes
Grants usually need not be paid back; some include training
Few are available; you must apply and meet the conditions; they take time
Buying equipment on credit (hire purchase)
Spreads the cost of a machine over time
Costs more in total; missed payments can lose you the item

blocks.p: **Interest** is the extra money you pay back on top of the amount you borrowed. Example: Jovaun borrows J$300 000 for a welding machine and tools. Over two years he pays back J$360 000 in total. The interest is J$360 000 − J$300 000 = J$60 000. Before you borrow, compare the **total** you will repay, not just the monthly payment, and make sure the business can pay it even in a slow month.

blocks.note: Borrow only from licensed or registered lenders, read every paper before you sign, and never borrow more than your plan shows you need. Spending all your savings on the first day, or borrowing as much as a lender will give you, raises the risk.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Banks, credit unions and micro-finance lenders all lend to small businesses in Jamaica, and public bodies such as the Jamaica Business Development Corporation (JBDC) offer advice and training to small businesses. What is on offer changes often: ask your instructor, and check the current terms before you apply.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Type
Owned by
Who pays the debts
Good points
Hard points
rows: **Sole trader**
One person
The owner, personally: their own savings, vehicle or home can be at risk
Simple and cheap to set up; the owner keeps all the profit and makes all the decisions
All the risk and work falls on one person; harder to raise money; the business may stop if the owner is ill
**Partnership**
Two or more partners who share the profits
The partners, usually personally and together
More money, skills and hands; the work is shared
Profits and decisions are shared; partners can disagree; one partner's debts and mistakes can fall on the others
**Limited company**
Shareholders, with directors running it
The company; owners usually risk only what they put in (limited liability)
Easier to raise money; it can carry on if owners change
More forms, costs and rules; accounts must be filed

blocks.p: Most tradespeople start as sole traders. Partners should always have a **written partnership agreement** that says who puts in what, how profits are shared, who decides what, and what happens if one partner leaves. **Employees** are the people who work for the business owner for a wage.

flow: Choose the type of business and a name
Register the business name (or form the company) with the Companies Office of Jamaica, so that the business is legal and its name is protected
Make sure you have a **TRN** (Taxpayer Registration Number) from Tax Administration Jamaica, and register for the taxes that apply to the business
Check whether your trade or your premises need a licence, permit or certificate
If you hire workers, register as an employer and pay their statutory deductions (such as NIS, NHT, education tax and income tax under PAYE) on time
Get suitable insurance and open a separate business bank account
Follow health and safety rules for your premises and your trade

head: Trade
Examples of what to check
rows: Electrical
Electrical work must be done by suitably licensed electricians, and new installations are inspected before the power is connected. Check the current rules with the Government Electrical Regulator.
Salon, barbering and beauty
Premises are usually approved by the public health department; check with the local health department and the municipal corporation (parish council).
Villa and food services
Anyone who prepares food for guests needs a food handler's permit from the health department.
Welding and fabrication
Large structures such as stairs, mezzanine floors or big canopies may need approved drawings or a building permit: check before you quote.

blocks.note: Rules, fees and forms change. Check the current requirements with the Companies Office of Jamaica, Tax Administration Jamaica and your municipal corporation (parish council) before you start, or ask a business adviser.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Insurance** helps cover losses from fire, theft, accidents and claims. You pay a regular amount (the premium); if the loss happens, the insurer pays part or all of it. Insurance does not make a business profitable and does not stop complaints: it stops one bad event from wiping the business out.

ul: **Property and equipment:** fire, theft and storm damage to your workshop, salon, tools and stock.
**Public liability:** if your work injures someone or damages their property, for example a gate falls on a car.
**Motor:** for any vehicle used for the business.

blocks.p: **Marketing** is everything you do to find customers, meet their needs and keep them coming back. It is much more than advertising.

head: P
The question
Mobile gate repair
Home nail service
rows: Product
What exactly do you sell, and to what standard?
Repairs to gates, grills and burglar bars: hinges, latches, rust repairs
Gel polish, acrylic sets, nail art, pedicures
Price
What will you charge, and how will people pay?
A call-out fee plus parts and labour; written quotes
A price list; bridal packages; a deposit when booking
Place
Where and how do customers get it?
At the customer's home, within about 15 km
In the client's home or a small studio; booking by phone or message
Promotion
How will customers hear about you?
Flyers in new housing schemes, photos online, word of mouth
Photos of work online, a referral discount, links with wedding planners

ul: **Word of mouth** is the best and cheapest promotion, and good work and good service earn it.
Social media and messaging-app posts with clear photos of your own work, your area and how to contact you.
Flyers and business cards at hardware stores, salons, churches and community notice boards (ask first).
A clear sign on your vehicle or premises.
A short **slogan** that people remember, such as "Strong gates, on time, every time".
A reward for referrals, such as a discount when a customer brings a friend.

blocks.p: Prime-time television adverts, daily newspaper pages and highway billboards cost far more than a new small business can earn back from them.

blocks.note: Only post photos of jobs you did yourself, and ask the customer before you show their home, their car or their face.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Happy customers come back and tell their friends; unhappy ones tell even more people. Answer calls and messages promptly, turn up when you say you will, give written quotes, keep the work area clean, explain what you did, and deal with complaints calmly and put things right.

head: Document
When
What it shows
rows: Quotation (quote)
Before the job starts
The work, materials, labour and total price; how long the price stands; payment terms; the date
Deposit
When the customer accepts the quote
A part-payment in advance that shows the customer is serious and helps buy materials; always give a receipt for it
Invoice (bill)
After the job, or at each stage
What was done, the amount due, any deposit already paid, and when payment is due
Receipt
When money is received
A written record that a payment was made: the date, the amount, what it was for, who paid and who received it

blocks.p: **Networking** means building contacts with people who can help your business: suppliers, contractors, villa and property managers, wedding planners, other tradespeople who can pass on work (customers often ask an electrician for a welder, and a welder for an electrician), past customers, trade associations, church and community groups, and your old instructors. Keep in touch, keep your word, and pass work on to others too.

sections.title: Records, risk and your business plan

blocks.p: Good records show whether the business is making a profit. They help you set prices, plan what to buy, spot problems early (such as a customer who has not paid), pay tax correctly, apply for a loan, and settle any disagreement with a customer or supplier.

head: Record
What it shows
rows: Cash book or sales book
Every amount received and paid out, each day
Copies of quotations, invoices and receipts
What was agreed, what was billed and what was paid
Bills and receipts for purchases
What you spent on materials, tools, rent, electricity and transport
Job cards
The work done for each customer, the materials used and the time taken
List of customers who owe money (debtors)
Who owes what, and since when
**Stock** list
The goods kept ready to use or sell: steel lengths, rods, cable, nail products, cleaning supplies
Wages record
Who was paid, how much, and the deductions made

ul: Keep business money and personal money apart, ideally with a separate business bank account.
Write up the cash book every day, while you remember.
Keep receipts in one place, sorted by month, and back up records kept on a phone.

blocks.note: Taking business money for personal spending makes it impossible to see how the business is really doing. Pay yourself a set wage instead.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Risk** is the chance of losing money or failing. You cannot remove all risk, but you can reduce it.

head: Risk
Ways to reduce it
rows: Too few customers at first
Do market research, test small, keep fixed costs low
Customers who do not pay
Written quotes, deposits, payments at stages, invoices sent on time and followed up
Fire, theft or hurricane damage
Insurance, secure storage, backed-up records, hurricane preparation
Equipment breaking down
Regular maintenance and some savings set aside for repairs
Prices of materials rising
Quotes that stand for a set time only (for example 14 days); check prices before quoting
The owner falling ill or getting hurt
Work safely; keep savings in reserve; have a trusted partner or helper
Competitors
Know them, have a clear selling point, keep quality and service high

blocks.note: Start small, plan well and keep good records. Spending all your savings at once, borrowing as much as you can, or ignoring the competition all raise the risk.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **business plan** is a written plan of the business: its goals, its market and its money. Writing it makes you think the idea through. Banks and other lenders read it to judge whether the business can pay back a loan.

head: Part
What it covers
rows: Summary
Business name, what it does, the owner and the main goals
Products or services
What you sell and to what standard
Market
Target customers, what your market research found, competitors and your USP
Marketing
Your prices and how you will reach customers
Operations
Location, equipment, materials, suppliers and any staff
Money
Start-up costs and where the money comes from; expected monthly sales and costs; cash flow; break-even
Goals and review
SMART goals for the first year and how progress will be checked

blocks.p: A plan is a working tool, not a form to file away. Every few months, compare what really happened with the plan, find out why they differ, and change the plan: your prices, your promotion, your costs or your goals.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor or your group.

ul: I can explain what an entrepreneur is and how self-employment differs from being employed.
I can name the qualities of a successful entrepreneur and say why each one matters.
I can explain why honest dealing is good for a small business.
I can do a SWOT analysis, putting strengths and weaknesses inside and opportunities and threats outside, and use it to plan.
I can write SMART goals for my savings, my skills and my business.
I can describe a sensible personal path from trainee to business owner.
I can spot a business opportunity and test it with a short survey and a study of competitors.
I can explain target market and unique selling point (USP).
I can sort costs into start-up, fixed and variable costs, with examples from my trade.
I can work out profit, a selling price with a percentage profit, and a break-even point.
I can explain cash flow and how deposits and stage payments help it.
I can name ways to raise start-up money, with an advantage and a disadvantage of each, and explain interest.
I can compare a sole trader, a partnership and a limited company.
I can list the main steps to set up legally in Jamaica, including registering the name and having a TRN.
I can use the four Ps and plan low-cost promotion.
I can explain what a quotation, a deposit, an invoice and a receipt are for.
I can list the records a small business should keep and why.
I can name business risks and ways to reduce them, including insurance.
I can list the parts of a simple business plan and explain why it should be reviewed.

terms: Break-even point
Where income just covers all the costs: no profit and no loss
Business opportunity
A need or problem that customers will pay to have met
Business plan
A written plan of the business's goals, market and money
Capital
Money put into a business to start or grow it; the owner's capital comes from their own savings
Cash flow
The money coming into and going out of a business, and when
Competitor
Another business selling the same or similar goods or services to the same customers
Deposit
Part of the price paid before a job starts, to show the customer is serious
Employee
A person who works for a business owner and is paid a wage
Entrepreneur
A person who starts and runs a business and takes the risk
Fixed cost
A cost that stays the same whatever the amount of work, such as rent
Four Ps
Product, price, place and promotion: the parts of marketing
Insurance
Regular payments that buy cover against losses from fire, theft, accidents and claims
Interest
The extra money paid back on top of the amount borrowed
Invoice
A document sent to the customer after a job, asking them to pay
Limited liability
When owners risk only what they put into the business, as in a limited company
Loan
Money borrowed, often from a bank or credit union, that must be paid back over time
Market research
Finding out about customers, competitors and demand
Networking
Building contacts with people who can help the business
Partnership
A business owned and run by two or more people who share the profits
Profit
The money left after all the costs are paid
Quotation (quote)
A written statement of the price, given before the job starts
Receipt
A written record that a payment was made
Risk
The chance of losing money or failing
Sales turnover
All the money received from sales, before costs are taken off
Self-employed
Working for yourself and taking the risk, instead of working for a wage
Slogan
A short, catchy phrase that helps people remember a business
SMART goal
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound
Sole trader
A business owned and run by one person
Start-up cost
A one-off cost of opening the business, such as the first machine and tools
Stock
Goods a business keeps ready to use or sell
Supplier
A business that sells you the materials you need
SWOT analysis
A look at strengths and weaknesses (inside) and opportunities and threats (outside)
Target market
The group of customers most likely to buy from you
TRN
Taxpayer Registration Number, issued by Tax Administration Jamaica
USP
Unique selling point: what makes your business different from the rest
Variable cost
A cost that goes up and down with the amount of work, such as materials

c1.title: A mobile grill-repair idea in Old Harbour
c1.text: Shamar, 23, finished his Level 2 welding course two years ago and works at a fabrication shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine. He wants to start a mobile service repairing gates, grills and burglar bars. He has his NVQ-J certificate, his own grinder and hand tools and J$85 000 saved, but no vehicle, and he has never priced a job on his own. A scheme of 400 new homes is being finished nearby, and two welders in the town already make new gates.

c2.title: Pricing a nail service in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: Shellian, a beauty therapy graduate in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, plans to rent a small room for J$28 000 a month and pay J$4 000 a month for her phone and internet. Each full set of acrylic nails uses about J$1 300 of products, and she plans to charge J$5 000 a set. The two salons in town charge J$4 500 and J$6 000 for a similar set.

c3.title: Two electricians team up in Port Antonio
c3.text: Romaine and Odean, both qualified electricians, plan to go into business together in Port Antonio, Portland, without forming a company. Romaine will put in J$400 000 and his van; Odean will put in J$150 000 and do most of the estimating. They want to hire a helper on a weekly wage. A hotel has asked them to quote for rewiring 12 rooms, a job that would need about J$900 000 of cable and fittings, with the hotel paying when the work is finished.

c4.title: A villa cleaning service near St Ann's Bay
c4.text: Nordia has worked for six years as a housekeeper at villas near St Ann's Bay, St Ann. Many of the villa owners live overseas and let their villas to visitors through property managers. Nordia plans to start her own cleaning and laundry service. She has very little money for advertising, and three cleaning services already work in the area.

c5.title: Quoting for burglar bars in Morant Bay
c5.text: Fitzroy runs a one-man welding business from his yard in Morant Bay, St Thomas. Mrs Gayle wants burglar bars for four windows, made from 16 mm square bar. Fitzroy works out the materials (steel, rods, discs, primer and paint) at J$36 000, his labour at 10 hours at J$1 400 an hour, and a share of his overheads at J$5 000. He adds 20% profit to the total cost. Fitzroy pays for his groceries from the same cash box he uses to buy steel, and the box is often short.

questions.q: Shamar is filling in a SWOT analysis. Which item belongs in his Opportunities box?
o: His J$85 000 in savings set aside for tools
Never having priced a job on his own
The scheme of 400 new homes nearby
The two welders in town who make gates
questions.why: Opportunities are chances outside Shamar that could help him: 400 new homes will need grills, gates and repairs. His savings are a strength and his lack of pricing practice a weakness (both inside him), and the two existing welders are a threat.

questions.q: Shamar's SWOT shows two weaknesses: no vehicle and no experience in pricing. What is the most sensible plan?
o: Buy a van on a loan at once, then learn pricing as he goes
Learn costing at work now, and use hired transport at first
Charge whatever the first customers offer until he learns
Wait until he can pay cash for a new van and a workshop
questions.why: A weakness is fixed by planning. He can learn costing from his supervisor while still employed and solve transport cheaply at first. A big loan before the idea is tested raises the risk, and guessed prices can lose money on every job.

questions.q: Shamar wants enough money for a used pickup. Which goal would let him track his progress month by month?
o: Save as much as possible until he can afford a pickup
Buy a good pickup some time in the next year or two
Save J$15 000 a month for 12 months, in a separate account
Put aside whatever is left over each month for transport
questions.why: This goal is specific, measurable (J$15 000 a month, J$180 000 in all), achievable on a wage, relevant to his transport weakness and time-bound (12 months). The others have no amount or no deadline, so he cannot tell whether he is on track.

questions.q: Shamar asks 12 relatives and church friends whether they would use his service. All 12 say yes. What is wrong with this market research?
o: Twelve answers are too many to count on a tally sheet
They are not a fair sample of his target customers
He should have asked the two other welders instead
Market research is only useful after the business opens
questions.why: Family and friends often say yes to please you, and most are not the people who will buy. He should ask homeowners in the new scheme and nearby, his target market, using short questions that do not lead them.

questions.q: Shellian expects to do 20 sets next month instead of 12. Which of her costs will go up?
o: The rent, since she will use the room more often
The phone and internet plan, since more clients will call
Every one of them, since all costs rise when work rises
The nail products, since each set uses its own
questions.why: Products are a variable cost: each set uses about J$1 300, so 20 sets use more than 12. The rent and the phone plan are fixed costs: she pays the same each month however many clients she has.

questions.q: How many full sets must Shellian do each month to break even?
o: 7 sets
8 sets
9 sets
25 sets
questions.why: Each set contributes J$5 000 − J$1 300 = J$3 700 towards her fixed costs of J$28 000 + J$4 000 = J$32 000. J$32 000 ÷ J$3 700 = 8.6, which rounds up to 9 sets: 8 sets would leave her J$2 400 short.

questions.q: A friend tells Shellian to charge J$3 500 a set to "beat the competition". What is the best reply?
o: Drop to J$3 500: the lowest price in town always brings the most clients
Keep J$5 000: it covers her costs with a profit and fits the local prices
Raise to J$6 500: clients always believe a dearer set is better quality
Match J$4 500: a new business must never charge more than the others
questions.why: A sound price covers all the costs, adds a profit and is checked against competitors. At J$3 500 she would need 15 sets a month just to break even, and anyone can undercut a low price; her selling point should be quality and service.

questions.q: A bride books Shellian to do the nails of her whole bridal party in three weeks' time, a J$32 000 job. What should Shellian ask for when the booking is made?
o: Nothing until the day, as asking for money may lose the booking
A written quotation from the bride stating what she will pay
A deposit, with a receipt, to hold the date and buy products
The full price in cash, with no receipt, to keep things simple
questions.why: A deposit shows the client is serious, protects Shellian if the booking is cancelled, and helps pay for products before the job is paid for. The receipt records the payment for both of them; the quotation comes from the business, not the client.

questions.q: Before they start, what is the most important document for Romaine and Odean to draw up together?
o: A written partnership agreement on money, work and profit shares
A price list showing what each of the 12 hotel rooms will cost
A slogan for the van that both partners have agreed to use
A list of their competitors and how much each one earns
questions.why: In a partnership, profits, decisions and usually debts are shared. As they put in unequal amounts, they must agree in writing how profits are split, who decides what and what happens if one leaves; this prevents most partnership quarrels.

questions.q: What is the main risk to each partner's own savings and property if the business runs up debts it cannot pay?
o: Only the partner who signed for a debt can ever be asked to pay it
The debts are limited to the J$550 000 the two of them put in
Their own property is safe once the business name is registered
Each partner can be made to pay the business's debts personally
questions.why: In an ordinary partnership the partners are usually personally liable for the business's debts, so their savings, vehicles or homes can be at risk. Limited liability comes with forming a company, not with registering a business name.

questions.q: Before the helper starts work, what must the business do?
o: Register as an employer so that it can pay his deductions
Ask the helper to pay all his own taxes and contributions
Pay him in cash with no records, to keep the books simple
Make him a partner so that no wage has to be paid to him
questions.why: An employer must register, deduct the statutory contributions and taxes (such as NIS, NHT, education tax and PAYE) from the wage, and pay them over on time. Paying cash with no records breaks the law and leaves the worker without cover.

questions.q: The hotel job needs about J$900 000 of materials before the hotel pays. What should the partners do to protect their cash flow?
o: Buy all the materials now and hope that the hotel pays early
Agree a deposit and payments at stages before starting
Lower the price so that the hotel will be sure to pay on time
Pay for the materials from the money kept for the helper's wages
questions.why: The business must pay for materials long before the hotel pays. A deposit and payments at agreed stages keep cash coming in; hoping for early payment or using wage money can leave the business unable to pay its bills.

questions.q: Which is the strongest unique selling point for Nordia's service?
o: Lower prices than the three services already working there
Cleaning to the same standard as the other services
A wider range of cleaning chemicals than the others carry
A photo report sent to each overseas owner after every clean
questions.why: A USP gives customers a reason to choose you over the rest. Owners who live abroad cannot see their villas, so photo reports meet a real need. A lower price is easy for a competitor to copy, and "the same standard" gives no reason to change.

questions.q: Where should Nordia spend her small promotion budget first?
o: Visits to property managers with a price list and references
A month of radio adverts at peak time across the island
Flyers handed out to tourists on the beach in the afternoon
A large roadside billboard on the main road for a year
questions.why: Her target market is villa owners and the property managers who look after their villas, so personal visits, references and networking reach the people who actually buy. Radio and billboards cost a lot and mostly reach people who will never need villa cleaning.

questions.q: To win her first contract, Nordia is tempted to use a cheaper, watered-down cleaner while charging for the dearer one. Why is this a bad business decision?
o: It is only wrong if the property manager writes it into the contract
Cheaper products always damage surfaces, so she would pay for repairs
One cheat found out can cost her many clients, as word travels fast
It is fine as long as the villa still looks clean when it is checked
questions.why: Customers paid for what was agreed, and cheating them is dishonest. In a small community word of a cheat travels fast among owners and managers, while repeat work and referrals come from trust.

questions.q: What price should Fitzroy put on the quotation?
questions.why: Total cost = J$36 000 + (10 × J$1 400 = J$14 000) + J$5 000 = J$55 000. Adding 20%: J$55 000 × 1.20 = J$66 000. Leaving out the overheads, or adding the profit to the materials only, would undercharge.

questions.q: Mrs Gayle accepts the quote. Halfway through, Fitzroy sees that 12 mm bar would save him J$6 000. What should he do?
o: Use the 12 mm bar and keep the saving, since she will not notice
Use the 12 mm bar only on the back windows, out of sight
Ask Mrs Gayle first, explaining the change and a lower price
Use the 16 mm bar but add J$6 000 to the bill for his trouble
questions.why: The accepted quote is an agreement. Changing the material without asking cheats the customer and makes the bars weaker; an honest owner explains the choice, offers the lower price and lets the customer decide.

questions.q: Fitzroy's cash box is often short when he needs to buy steel. Which change would help most?
o: Keep a bigger cash box so that more money fits in at once
Open a business account and pay himself a set weekly wage
Stop giving receipts so that customers pay him faster
Buy steel only after each customer has paid in full
questions.why: Mixing household and business spending hides how the business is doing and drains the money meant for materials. A separate account and a set wage keep the two apart and let him plan both.

questions.q: Which of these people is self-employed?
o: A hotel electrician who is paid a fixed salary at the end of every month
A barber who rents a chair, finds his own clients and keeps the profit
A welder who works a set shift at a steel shop and is paid each Friday
A villa housekeeper hired by a property manager on a weekly wage
questions.why: Self-employed people work for themselves, find their own customers and carry the risk: the barber earns only what his clients pay, less his chair rent. The others are employees on a wage or salary.

questions.q: Six months after opening, Tanisha's sales are 30% below the forecast in her business plan. What should she do?
o: Compare her results with the plan, find out why, and change it
Ignore the plan, since it was only needed to get her bank loan
Borrow more money so that next month's sales figure can be met
Close the business, since a plan that is not met means failure
questions.why: A business plan is a working tool. Reviewing it every few months shows where you are behind and why, so you can change prices, promotion or costs in time. Borrowing does not create sales.
